title: JavaScript Jam x React Miami: Announcing Miami Jam, a Game Show for the React Community
outline: Introduction and context: a Twitter Space stumble, a lesson in patience, and the kickoff of a special episode
What JavaScript Jam Live is: an open mic for JavaScript and web development where every skill level participates
The React Miami collaboration: introducing Ishan Anand, Anthony Campolo, Scott Steinlage, Dev Agrawal, and organizer Michelle
Miami Jam: replacing the standard interview panel with a trivia-driven game show
How the format works: React and JavaScript trivia, speaker-to-speaker questions, and segues into deeper discussion
Why a game show format works for conference content
Audience participation as a core mechanic: asking questions and awarding points
Lessons from going live: technical resilience and community humor
What's next and how to join in: upcoming speakers, surprises, and an open invitation
draft: Every live show has an origin story, and this week's episode of JavaScript Jam Live began with a classic one: a Twitter Space that appeared to start on the host's phone while the audience saw nothing at all. After a minute or two of patience, everything clicked into place, the room filled up, and the show rolled on. It was a minor stumble with a useful lesson for anyone hosting live audio — sometimes the platform just needs a moment to catch up — and it set the tone for an episode that was equal parts practical, playful, and community-driven.## An Open Mic for the Web CommunityJavaScript Jam Live describes itself as an open mic for anything JavaScript and web development related, and the description fits. Beginners and veterans are equally welcome to grab the mic, ask questions, share opinions, or drop facts into the conversation. The hosts made a point of it during this episode: whether you have been building for the web for decades or you are just getting started, your voice adds value. In their experience, some of the best conversations happen precisely when the audience steps up and participates, turning a broadcast into a genuine discussion.## A Special Collaboration with React MiamiThis week marked the kickoff of something special: a collaboration with React Miami that Scott playfully rebranded as 'React Miami Month.' Over the coming weeks, JavaScript Jam will feature speakers from the React Miami lineup discussing topics that connect naturally with their conference talks, while keeping the show's traditional open-mic vibe intact. As the team put it, nothing about the show changes — there is simply more value for the audience and a few extra goodies still to be revealed.The episode doubled as a roll call of the people making it happen. Ishan Anand, VP of Product at Edgio, an edge deployment platform, hosts the show. Anthony Campolo, developer advocate at Edgio, and Scott Steinlage, technical community manager at Edgio, round out the crew. They were joined by Dev Agrawal, a media partner for React Miami helping organize events, activities, and content, and by Michelle, one of the organizers of React Miami herself, who admitted the team had essentially been given the green light to do whatever they like with the partnership. Whether she ends up regretting that trust, she joked, remains to be seen.## Miami Jam: A Game Show, Not a PanelThe centerpiece of the announcement is Miami Jam, a live show Dev dreamed up and roped Anthony and Scott into hosting. The idea is simple but refreshing: instead of the typical interview or panel format, where speakers field a string of predictable questions one after another, Miami Jam is structured like a game show.Trivia is the engine. Questions might cover React itself, the weird quirks of JavaScript and TypeScript, adjacent tooling, or challenges like guessing which library is being used based on clues. Some questions will even target one speaker's topic and be directed at another speaker, who has to answer on the fly. From there, the trivia becomes a springboard: each answer opens the door to deeper discussion about the speaker's actual conference talk, the motivation behind it, their experience in the industry, and the work that brings them to React Miami in the first place.The goal is a show that is more fun, more interactive, and more collaborative than a standard panel — one where speakers share experiences with each other rather than performing serially for the audience.## Why a Game Show Format WorksConference content tends to follow a familiar rhythm: introduction, talk, Q&A, next speaker. It works, but it rarely surprises anyone. A game show breaks that rhythm. Trivia creates stakes, humor, and memorable moments; it reveals how speakers think under pressure rather than how they rehearse. Asking one speaker about another's topic forces genuine listening and produces the kind of cross-pollination that scripted panels seldom achieve. And because the trivia is grounded in React, JavaScript, and TypeScript oddities, the entertainment carries real technical substance — viewers learn something even when they are just laughing at a wrong answer.## The Audience Gets to Play TooCrucially, Miami Jam is not just a spectacle for spectators. Audience members can ask their own questions, but they can also shape the game itself. In one proposed mechanic, when an audience member poses a question to a speaker, that audience member also decides how many points the speaker earns for the answer. It is a small twist, but it hands real power to the crowd and blurs the line between stage and seats. For a show built on audience participation, that fits perfectly.## Lessons from Going LiveBeyond the announcements, the episode offered a warm, unfiltered look at live production. The opening delay became a teaching moment: hosts learned that a Twitter Space can appear to start locally while remaining invisible to listeners, and that waiting a minute or two usually resolves it. Scott shrugged it off with good humor, noting that no matter how much you know about tech, there is always something ready to make you look like a fool. Another participant invoked the old Titanic demotivational poster: maybe your role is to be a lesson for others. The audience's patience and good cheer turned a technical hiccup into a bonding moment — exactly the kind of resilience live community events are built on.## What's Next and How to Join InThe React Miami collaboration is just beginning. In the weeks ahead, expect more speakers from the conference to appear on JavaScript Jam Live, more game-show style segments, and a few surprises the team is saving for later. The open mic stays open, but the partnership adds more reasons than ever to show up live.If you want to take part, the invitation is open: request the mic, ask a question, share an opinion, or simply enjoy watching experienced developers sweat over JavaScript trivia. Miami Jam is happening soon, and the best game shows are the ones where the audience helps write the outcome. Come play.
